opus-5.5.text:
I think the word "systematically" is the key, because a lot of organizations can do AI in a scattered way. They have a few very strong people, each pushing their own idea, and sometimes that produces a breakthrough. But doing it systematically is different. It means the organization, not just individuals, is reliably turning compute, data, and people into better models, again and again.

A few things matter most to me.

First is clarity about what you're actually optimizing. In frontier model work there are many directions that look interesting: a new architecture, a new RL trick, a new data source. A systematic organization has a fairly sharp view of what the main bottleneck is right now and points most of its effort there. That doesn't mean no exploration, but exploration is deliberate, not just whatever people happen to find fun.

Second is infrastructure and evaluation, which I think people underrate. If your experiments are slow, hard to reproduce, or your evals don't track what you care about, you can't learn quickly. A lot of the advantage of the strongest labs isn't one secret idea. It's that a researcher can test a hypothesis cleanly, at the right scale, and trust the result. That's what lets knowledge compound instead of everyone rediscovering the same things.

Third is how scale changes research. Coming from physics, I noticed a big culture shift. In physics you can often make progress alone with a notebook. In large-model research, the important experiments are expensive and touch many parts of the system: pretraining, post-training, data, infra. So you need people willing to work as part of a larger machine, sharing credit, writing things down, making their work usable by others. Individual brilliance still matters a lot, but it has to plug into the whole.

Fourth is honesty, almost scientific integrity at the organizational level. When an experiment fails, people need to say so clearly, and when a direction isn't working, leadership needs to be willing to cut it even if it was someone's favorite. Organizations that can't absorb negative results end up chasing noise.

Finally, I'd say taste and conviction at the top. Being systematic doesn't mean bureaucratic. Someone still has to make big bets, like how much compute to put into a new paradigm before it's proven. The best organizations combine that kind of conviction with very disciplined execution underneath. So to me, doing AI systematically is less about having the single smartest person and more about building an environment where good ideas reliably get found, tested, and scaled.

r002.rationale: It describes testing hypotheses and evaluating results, but does not identify distinguishing factors associated with a change from those that are not.

r003.rationale: The response says evaluations should track what matters, but does not mention that metrics can be gamed to make work look better.

r004.rationale: It mentions testing at the right scale, but does not frame checking whether promising results remain truly good at scale as a responsibility of trustworthy practitioners.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing people get wrong is that they treat "doing AI systematically" as a matter of hiring a lot of smart people and buying a lot of compute. Those are necessary, but they're not what makes it systematic. What makes it systematic is that the organization has a clear idea of what the bottleneck is, and it organizes everything around that bottleneck rather than around what's fashionable.

Let me give an example. For a long time, the bottleneck in AI was ideas and algorithms. You could have a small group of people, a few GPUs, and if you had the right idea you could change the field. Then the bottleneck shifted to scaling: data, compute, infrastructure, engineering discipline. The organizations that did well in that era were not necessarily the ones with the best researchers in the classical sense. They were the ones who could turn research into something that runs reliably at huge scale, who could iterate quickly, who treated infrastructure as a first-class problem rather than something you outsource.

Now I think we're in a transition again. With language models being this capable, the bottleneck is increasingly about environments and evaluation, about defining the tasks that matter and building ways to measure progress on them. If you don't know how to measure what you're doing, you can't do it systematically, almost by definition. So a big part of doing AI well now is building good evals, good environments, good feedback loops between the model and the real world. That sounds unglamorous, but it is where a lot of the actual leverage is.

The second thing is people. An organization needs people who can move between layers. Someone who only understands the algorithm, or only understands the infrastructure, or only understands the product, will make locally reasonable decisions that are globally wrong. The best teams I've seen have a few people who can see the whole stack, who can tell you why a product requirement implies a certain training setup, which implies certain data, which implies certain infrastructure choices. You don't need everyone to be like that, but you need enough of them in the right places.

Third is taste about time horizons. Systematic doesn't mean slow. It means you have a long-term direction, but you take many short, honest steps toward it, and you're willing to be wrong on each step. A lot of organizations either chase every new paper and have no direction, or they lock onto a five-year roadmap and refuse to update when the evidence changes. Neither is systematic. Systematic is having a hypothesis about where things are going, running experiments that could falsify it, and actually updating.

And finally, I think culture matters more than process. You can write down any process you want, but if people are rewarded for looking impressive rather than for finding out what's true, the process won't save you. The organizations that do AI well tend to have a culture where a negative result is still a result, where a junior person can say the flagship approach isn't working and be taken seriously, and where the question "how do we know?" is asked constantly. If you have that, the rest is mostly engineering. If you don't have that, no amount of compute will make you systematic.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to connect AI capabilities to a real feedback loop. It’s relatively easy for an organization to build a demo. It’s much harder to know whether that demo is improving the work people actually do, and then to keep improving it systematically.

So I would start with a concrete task: What does success look like? What information does the system need? What actions can it take? How do you tell when it has made a mistake? Those questions require people who understand the business to work closely with people who understand the technology. You can’t simply hand everything to an AI team and expect them to figure it out.

Then you need a way to turn experience into progress. If the system fails, can you capture that failure, understand it, and use it to evaluate the next version? Otherwise, you’re changing prompts or models based on impressions. You might get a better-looking answer without actually getting a better system.

There’s also an organizational question: are you willing to change the workflow? If you only add AI to an existing process, the benefit may be limited. But redesigning everything immediately is risky too. I’d begin with a bounded task, establish that it works, and gradually give the system more responsibility.

To me, doing AI systematically means building that whole cycle: choosing useful problems, deploying something, measuring what happens, and learning from it. The model is one component. The organization’s ability to run that cycle is what makes the capability durable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to distinguish using AI tools from building an organization around AI. You can give everyone access to a model, and that might improve individual productivity, but it doesn’t automatically change how the organization works.

To do it systematically, you need a loop: identify a useful task, give the AI the context and tools to attempt it, evaluate the result, and use what you learn to improve the system. The evaluation part is especially important. If you don’t know what a good outcome looks like, it’s very hard to know whether a more capable model is actually helping.

And this isn’t only an engineering problem. The people who understand the work need to collaborate closely with the people building the AI system. You need someone who owns the outcome, because otherwise you can end up with lots of impressive demos that never become part of everyday work.

So I would start with a concrete workflow, make it work reliably, and then expand. Over time, the organization develops the infrastructure and the habits to keep doing that. To me, that repeatable ability is what makes the effort systematic.
